'''Carl-Wilhelm Reinhold de Boor''' (born 3 December 1937) is an American [[mathematician]] and professor emeritus at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2005-03-14 |title=Top scientists honored at White House |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna7182001 |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref> In 1993, he was elected as a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] for contributions to numerical analysis and methods in particular numerical tools used in [[computer-aided design]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Dr. Carl R. de Boor |url=https://nae.edu/27649/Dr-Carl-R-de-Boor |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=NAE Website |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life==
'''de Boor''' was born in [[Stolp]], Germany (now [[Słupsk]], Poland), in 1937, as the seventh of eight children born to Werner (an anti-Nazi Lutheran minister) and Toni de Boor.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Carl de Boor - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/De_Boor/ |access-date=2026-04-23 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> The family fled in 1945, settling in [[Schwerin]], then part of [[East Germany]].<ref name=":0" /> He stayed in West Germany when his application to study chemistry at [[Humboldt University]] in [[East Berlin]] was turned down.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Carl R. de Boor |url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/carl-r-de-boor/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> He was supported by [[Otto Friedrich]], the brother of Carl's father's first wife. Two years later, he began a romantic relationship with Otto's niece, Matilda Friedrich, the daughter of political scientist [[Carl Friedrich]].<ref name=":0" /> With the support of the Friedrich family, Carl emigrated to the United States in 1959, learning English on his trip across the Atlantic.<ref name=":2" />

==Education and career==
[[File:Carl de Boor - National Medal of Science, 2005.webm|thumb|de Boor discussing his life and career.]]
Having left [[Hamburg University]] without a degree, de Boor enrolled as a mathematics graduate student at [[Harvard University|Harvard]]. He worked briefly as a research assistant to [[Garrett Birkhoff]] before joining [[General Motors Research Laboratories|General Motors Research]] in [[Warren, Michigan]], where he first encountered [[splines]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=de Boor and Luce Receive National Medal of Science |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200506/comm-medal.pdf |website=American Mathematical Society}}</ref> He earned his Ph.D. from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1966, then joined [[Purdue University]] as an [[assistant professor]]. In 1972, he moved to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] as a professor of mathematics and computer science, based at the Army Math Research Center.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carl R. de Boor {{!}} Department of Applied Mathematics {{!}} University of Washington |url=https://amath.washington.edu/people/carl-r-de-boor |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=amath.washington.edu}}</ref>

==Retirement and personal life==

Carl de Boor retired from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 2003 and relocated to [[Orcas Island]] in [[Washington (state)|Washington]] state, with his second wife, author [[Helen Bee]], who he married in 1991.<ref name=":3" /> He is also an affiliated professor at the [[University of Washington]].<ref>[http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi?&link1=Browse&link2=Results&id=2487 ISI Highly Cited Author - Carl R. de Boor] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060304073635/http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi?&link1=Browse&link2=Results&id=2487|date=March 4, 2006}}</ref>

==Awards==
De Boor was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 1997, and received the 2003 [[National Medal of Science]] in [[mathematics]].<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5000000000425 National Science Foundation - The President's National Medal of Science]</ref> Other honors have included election to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1987<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Academy of Arts and Sciences – UW-Madison Members |url=https://provost.wisc.edu/uw-madison-highly-prestigious-award-recipients/american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences-uw-madison-members/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=Office of the Provost |language=en-US}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1993,<ref>{{Cite web |title=NAE Award |url=https://www.nae.edu/File.aspx?id=323166 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250724044544/https://www.nae.edu/File.aspx?id=323166 |archive-date=2025-07-24 |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=www.nae.edu |url-status=live }}</ref> honorary degrees from [[Purdue University]] and [[Technion]] (the Israel Institute of Technology), as well as membership in the [[German Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] in Germany and the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-03-25 |title=Research Team from Corning Incorporated Earn Nation’s Highest Honor for Accomplishments - UNews Archive |url=https://archive.unews.utah.edu/news_releases/research-team-from-corning-incorporated-earn-nation039s-highest-honor-for-accomplishments/ |access-date=2025-11-25 |website=archive.unews.utah.edu |language=en-US}}</ref> He won the [[John von Neumann Prize|John von Neumann Lecture Prize]] from the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] in 1996 and the [[John A. Gregory Award of Geometric Design]] in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2024-06-22|title=John A. Gregory Memorial Award|url=https://www.geometric-modelling.org/gregory-award/index.html|access-date=2025-12-13|website=www.geometric-modelling.org|language=en-US}}</ref>
